03 — Healthcare Platform · MyPulse

MyPulse — Diagnostics, Doctors & Care in One Platform

Sole UX Designer · End-to-end, zero to shipped product
RoleSole UX designer — research to shipped UI
SurfacesConsumer web, mobile app, doctor console, admin
UsersPatients, doctors, labs, pharmacies, scan centres
Live atmypulse.co.in
Background

Healthcare booking, minus the phone calls.

Booking a scan in India usually means calling labs one at a time to ask what they charge and when they're free. MyPulse replaces that with a single platform where a patient can find nearby diagnostic labs, compare prices, book tests and scans, find a doctor by speciality, and order from a pharmacy — with the whole thing also running as a mobile app.

I joined as the only designer on it and stayed the only designer on it. Every surface below — the consumer site, the app, the console doctors work in, the admin back office — came out of the same pair of hands, which meant the system had to stay coherent without a team to enforce it.

The surfaces

Four audiences, one product.

Healthcare marketplaces fail when the supply side is an afterthought. Patients only get same-day slots if labs, doctors and scan centres have tools they'll actually keep updated — so the professional surfaces got the same attention as the consumer one.

Consumer — web

Responsive marketplace

The public product: search by test, scan or speciality, compare labs near you, and book.

  • Lab test and scan discovery by category and location
  • Doctor discovery across ten specialities
  • Cart and checkout for multi-test bookings
  • Health packages, pharmacy and home care
Consumer — mobile

Native app

The same journeys designed for the phone, where most bookings actually happen.

  • Location-first search and booking
  • Reports and booking history in one place
  • Promoted throughout the site as the primary channel
Supply — doctors

Doctor console

Where practitioners run their day: patients, prescriptions and communication.

  • Patient detail and history views
  • Prescription (Rx) creation flow
  • Appointment and availability management
  • Communication templates for patient messaging
Supply — operators

Admin & partners

The back office that keeps the marketplace stocked and correct.

  • Super admin and business admin roles
  • Plan selection and subscription management
  • Pharmacy fulfilment flow
  • Scan centre onboarding and management

Booking journey

Four steps, stated on the page.

The homepage commits to the journey out loud — "4 easy steps to get your solution" — which set a hard constraint on the design: if the flow needed a fifth step, the promise on the front page was wrong.

Final UI

The shipped product.

Screens pulled directly from the design files — registration across four business types, the full doctor-booking journey from search to confirmed payment, the seven-step clinic onboarding wizard, family management, doctor records, verification and error states, and subscriptions, all from the same component language.

MyPulse — consumer app, shipped design

WelcomeDoctor-facing splash, one of a rotating set of audience states.
Sign inCountry-code aware phone entry, full picker rather than a guess.
Add family memberOne form covering identity, contact and full address in a single pass.
AccountProfile, mPIN, notifications and terms — the account settings hub.
Doctor — detailsSpeciality, gender and clinic address laid out before any booking action.
Doctor — historySame header, second tab — prior visits with diagnosis at a glance.
AppointmentsOne list, three order types — scan, pharmacy and doctor — behind a single filter.
Visit recordVitals, systemic exam, complaints, diagnosis and prescription in one structured record.
Family — detailsA dependent profile: DOB, blood group, relation, address.
Family — appointmentsThat dependent’s visit history, addressed by name.
Family — doctorsDoctors this family member has seen, with history one tap away.

MyPulse for doctors — the console I designed alongside the consumer app

Doctor — homeWeek strip, today’s appointments, and a switch between clinic appointments and preferred pharmacies.
Doctor — quick actionsThe same screen mid-gesture: a radial menu for jumping straight to patients, appointments or writing a prescription.
Doctor — empty stateNo appointments for the selected day — designed rather than left blank.

Booking a doctor — search to confirmed, eight real screens

1 · SearchAssigned doctors with clinic, next slot and phone number, book straight from the list.
2 · Doctor profileTimings for every day of the week and a location map, before committing to a booking.
3 · Appointment typeOn-call, video or in-clinic — the same doctor, three ways to actually be seen.
4 · DateMorning through night bands above a full calendar, for people who think in either.
5 · Time slotUnavailable slots visibly greyed rather than simply missing.
6 · SummaryType, day-part and exact time confirmed once more before money changes hands.
7 · PaymentPay now or pay at the centre, with saved-card support through Razorpay.
8 · ConfirmedAn appointment ID and an itemised fee, not just a checkmark.

Security & access

Sign-in — mPINNumeric PIN with a show/hide toggle and a recovery path, not just a password field re-skinned.

Getting started — four kinds of business, one registration system

Register asOne flow, four business types — consumer, doctor, pharmacy, or scan and diagnostic centre.
Business profileInline validation on a real field, not just on submit.
Doctor profileMCI number and state council sit alongside speciality — fields a generic sign-up form wouldn’t have.
Account setupWhat’s live sits beside what’s roadmap — stated on the screen itself.

Verification, notifications & error handling

OTP — error stateInvalid code, with the resend timer still counting down underneath.
mPIN — error stateSame pattern applied to the PIN step, so the two verification moments feel like one system.
Notification settingsPush, email and SMS controlled separately for appointments, medicines and family updates.
Rx — error modalA blocking error inside prescription creation, the one place a silent failure would matter most.

Plans & subscriptions

Plan — onboardingStep 1 of 7 — plans introduced as part of setup, not bolted on afterwards.
Plan — renewalThe same plan structure later, as a renewal screen with configurable add-ons.

Setting up a clinic — the seven-step business wizard

OverviewSeven steps, always visible, with completed ones marked — the clinic can see exactly where they are.
Operating hoursEvery day configurable independently, with a plain-language time picker.
Visiting hours — weeklyPer-day open and close times, multiple ranges, closed days, and a 24-hour option in one row.
Visiting hours — monthlySame step, calendar view — for a clinic that thinks in dates rather than weekdays.
Custom time ruleA recurrence choice — same day every month, same date every month, or once — for the schedule that doesn’t fit the default.
Add doctor / staffRoles assigned as people are invited, not bolted on afterwards.
Add existing patientsA clinic migrating from paper can seed its patient list before going live.
My role

Sole designer, start to finish.

What I owned
  • Research and problem definition across patients, doctors and lab operators
  • Information architecture for the consumer marketplace and the professional consoles
  • Wireframes and prototypes for every surface — web, mobile, doctor, admin
  • Final UI and the component set holding all four surfaces together
  • Handoff and build support through to launch
What being the only designer meant
  • No design team to enforce consistency, so the system had to be simple enough for me to hold in my head and for engineers to apply without me
  • Prioritisation was constant — four surfaces, one designer, one roadmap
  • Working directly with engineering rather than through a design lead
  • Decisions had to be defensible on their own; there was no second designer to sanity-check them
